name: Somarama (Someswara Temple)
deity: Shiva is worshipped here as Someswara Swamy in the form of a lingam that is said to change hue with the phases of the moon. The goddess is venerated as Sri Rajarajeswari, and Annapurna is also honoured at the site.
style: Dravidian temple architecture with later additions
summary: Somarama at Gunupudi on the edge of Bhimavaram is one of the five Pancharama Kshetras, a group of Shaiva shrines revered across the Godavari-Krishna delta. Its presiding deity is Someswara Swamy, worshipped as a lingam that is said to shift in colour through the lunar month. An unusual upper shrine to Vishnu above the Shiva sanctum sets the temple apart.

sections.history: Somarama is counted among the Pancharama Kshetras, five ancient Shaiva centres of the Andhra coastal region whose linked traditions place them within a shared body of legend. The present temple at Gunupudi is generally associated with the patronage of the Eastern Chalukyas, a dynasty active in the region around the tenth century, and building activity is often linked with a ruler remembered as Chalukya Bhima. Like many long-worshipped sites, the structure reflects successive phases of care and addition by later patrons and communities. Over the centuries it has remained a living place of worship rather than a monument, drawing pilgrims who travel the circuit of the five shrines and local devotees who observe its seasonal festivals.
sections.architecture: The temple is arranged around the sanctum of Someswara Swamy, above which rises a distinctive upper shrine dedicated to Vishnu as Janardana Swamy, a vertical pairing of Shiva and Vishnu that is rarely seen and gives the building much of its character. The plan follows the broad conventions of southern temple design, with a pillared hall leading toward the inner sanctum and a gopura marking the entrance. A large temple tank associated with the site, known as the Chandra Pushkarini, lies nearby and features in ritual and legend. Stone and masonry work from different periods can be read across the complex, testifying to the long span over which the temple has been maintained and enlarged.
sections.legends: The temple's name recalls Chandra, the moon god also called Soma, who in the Pancharama tradition is said to have installed and worshipped the lingam here, an act that gives Somarama its name. The lingam's reputed change of colour through the lunar month, paler around the full moon and darker toward the new moon, is understood as an echo of this bond with the moon. The wider legend traces the five lingams of the Pancharama shrines to a single great lingam associated with the story of Tarakasura, which is said to have broken into pieces that came to rest at five places. Each fragment was then established and worshipped by a different divine figure, Somarama being the share linked with Soma.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the temple's principal festival, observed with night-long worship and a Kalyanotsavam that ceremonially celebrates the marriage of the deities. The month of Karthika, sacred to Shiva, brings sustained observance with lamp offerings and larger gatherings, and the Navaratri season devoted to the goddess is marked with special worship of Sri Rajarajeswari. On these occasions the temple and its tank draw pilgrims from the surrounding delta towns as well as those completing the wider Pancharama circuit. Dates follow the traditional lunar calendar and shift from year to year, so devotees planning to attend are advised to confirm the schedule locally.
sections.experience: A visit to Somarama tends to be unhurried. The temple sits at Gunupudi on the edge of Bhimavaram, close enough to the town's daily life yet set within its own quiet precinct beside the temple tank. Many devotees pause first at the tank before entering, then move through the pillared hall toward the sanctum, where the lingam's association with the changing moon lends the darshan a particular resonance for those who visit across different phases of the lunar month. The glance upward to the Vishnu shrine is part of what regular visitors describe. Mornings and festival evenings are the busiest and most atmospheric times, while ordinary afternoons offer a calmer, more contemplative visit.

visit.timings: The temple generally opens in the early morning and again in the evening, with a midday break, following the customary pattern for temples in the region. Exact hours vary by day and season and around festivals, so it is best to verify the current timings locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Modest, traditional dress is expected, as at other temples in the region. Visitors typically remove footwear before entering the inner areas; covering the shoulders and legs is appreciated.
visit.photography: Photography rules vary and are often restricted within the sanctum and inner shrines. Look for posted signs and ask temple staff before taking photographs, particularly near the deities.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is at Gunupudi in Bhimavaram, West Godavari district. Bhimavaram is well connected by rail and road, and the town is easily reached from across the delta; the nearest airports are at Rajahmundry and Vijayawada.
